b2013-2.ask: Diana's cube is complete. Nathalie built only part of it. How many small cubes are missing?
steps: Look at the cube one layer at a time, from back to front. Don't try to count everything at once.
The back layer is complete. Nothing missing there.
The middle layer is missing 2 cubes.
The front layer is missing 5 cubes. Total missing: 2 + 5 = 7.
b2013-2.check: The full cube has 27 cubes. Count the cubes in Figure 2: you should get 20. 27 − 20 = 7. ✓
b2013-2.spot: 3D counting? Slice the shape into layers and count one layer at a time.
b2013-2.oops: Forgetting cubes hidden at the back or underneath.

b2013-3.ask: On the line from Mara to Bunica, the 1/8 mark is 100 m from Mara. How far is it to Bunica?
steps: The mark at 1/8 means: 100 m is one eighth of the whole way.
If one eighth is 100 m, all eight eighths are 8 × 100 m.
b2013-3.check: 1/4 would be 200 m and 1/2 would be 400 m. Those match the marks on the line. ✓
b2013-3.spot: Know one piece and how many pieces make the whole? Multiply.
b2013-3.oops: Using the 1/4 or 1/2 mark as if it were 100 m.

b2013-4.ask: Nick can only turn right. What's the fewest turns to get from A to B on the map?
steps: Trace routes with your finger. Every turn must be to the right.
To go left, you'd have to turn right 3 times (around a block). That costs a lot, so avoid it.
Look for a route that loops around the outside of the blocks, turning right at each corner.
The best route needs 4 right turns.
b2013-4.check: Try routes with 3 turns: none reach B. 4 turns works. ✓
b2013-4.spot: Maps with rules? Trace it with your finger, counting carefully, and try a few routes.
b2013-4.oops: Sneaking in a left turn without noticing.

b2013-5.ask: Ann, Bob and Chris are 31 years old in total. What will the total be in 3 years?
steps: In 3 years, EACH person is 3 years older.
3 people × 3 years = 9 more years in total.
b2013-5.spot: Ages added together? Birthdays come for everyone: add the years once for each person.
b2013-5.oops: Adding only 3 (34). Everyone gets older, not just one person.

b2013-6.ask: The same digit goes in all three boxes: ▢▢ × ▢ = 176. Which digit?
steps: Try the answer choices, or look for 176 = (two-digit number) × (one digit).
We need the same digit everywhere: 44 × 4 uses only 4s!
b2013-6.spot: Only five choices? Try them. Testing is often the fastest way.
b2013-6.oops: Picking 8 because 22 × 8 = 176. But the digits must all be the same.

b2013-7.ask: A pill every 15 minutes, the first at 11:05. When is the fourth pill?
steps: List the times: 1st 11:05.
b2013-7.check: From the 1st to the 4th pill there are 3 gaps: 3 × 15 = 45 minutes. 11:05 + 45 min = 11:50. ✓
b2013-7.spot: Counting events in a row? Count the GAPS: 4 pills have 3 gaps between them.

b2013-8.ask: Two circles can make 3 regions. What's the most regions two squares can make?
steps: To make lots of regions, the squares should cross each other as many times as possible.
Turn one square 45° over the other, like a star.
Each of the 8 points of the star is its own small region.
Plus the middle where both squares overlap: 8 + 1 = 9.
b2013-8.check: Draw it: a square and the same square turned, centres together. Count: 8 triangles + 1 middle = 9. ✓
b2013-8.spot: Most regions or pieces? Make the lines cross as many times as you can.
b2013-8.oops: Just shifting one square over the other, which only makes 3 regions.

b2013-9.ask: How many numbers between 20 and 30 can be divided exactly by their own ones digit?
steps: Check each number from 21 to 29.
Four of them work: 21, 22, 24, 25.
b2013-9.check: Go back over the four ✓ numbers: each divides exactly. ✓
b2013-9.spot: Small range? Check each one in order so you don't skip any.

b2013-10.ask: How many T-shaped pieces (4 squares each) can fit in a 4 × 5 rectangle without overlapping?
steps: The rectangle has 20 squares. 5 pieces would need all 20, every single square covered.
Colour the rectangle like a checkerboard: 10 black, 10 white.
A T-piece always covers 3 of one colour and 1 of the other. Try it!
With 5 pieces, the colours can never come out 10 and 10. So 5 is impossible, but 4 pieces do fit.
b2013-10.check: Draw 4 T-pieces in the rectangle: it's easy to fit them, with 4 squares left over. ✓
b2013-10.spot: Can these pieces fill a shape? A checkerboard colouring often shows it's impossible.
b2013-10.oops: Dividing 20 by 4 = 5 and stopping there. Fitting is trickier than area.

b2013-11.ask: Each piece is a chain of joined circles. Which piece covers the most dots in the table?
steps: Colour the table cells like a checkerboard. Moving one cell sideways or up/down always switches colour.
So two dots that are an even number of steps apart are on the same colour, and an odd number of steps apart are on different colours.
Do the same on each piece: colour its circles in two colours, switching at every step. The dots it can cover must all be one colour.
Count the bigger colour group on each piece: A 4, B 4, C 5, D 4, E 3. Piece C can cover 5.
b2013-11.check: Place C on the table: all 5 of its same-colour circles land on dots. ✓
b2013-11.spot: Grid puzzles? A checkerboard colouring can show patterns you didn't notice.
b2013-11.oops: Counting circles instead of checking how many can land on dots at the same time.

b2013-12.ask: Mary shades different shapes on square sheets. How many shapes have the same perimeter as the whole square?
steps: Each shaded shape's outline is made of some edges of the square plus some lines inside the square.
For each inside line, look for a matching piece of the square's edge that the shape doesn't use, the same length and direction.
If every inside line has a match, the perimeter is the same as the square's. If any line is left over, the perimeter is longer.
Four shapes have every inside line matched.
b2013-12.check: Slide each matched inside line out onto the edge it matches: you get the square's outline exactly. ✓
b2013-12.spot: Perimeter of shapes with steps? Slide the edges out to the edges.
b2013-12.oops: Thinking a smaller area means a smaller perimeter.

b2013-13.ask: Ann rides at a steady speed. The clocks show when she starts and finishes. Where is the minute hand after one third of the ride?
steps: Read the clocks: she starts at 1:30 and finishes at 3:30. The ride takes 2 hours = 120 minutes.
One third of 120 minutes = 40 minutes.
At 2:10, the minute hand points at the 2.
b2013-13.spot: Fractions of time? Change hours to minutes first.
b2013-13.oops: Taking a third of 2 hours as 0.33 hours and getting confused. Minutes are easier.

b2013-14.ask: If Matthew had caught 3 times as many fish, he'd have 12 more than he does. How many did he catch?
steps: 3 times his fish compared with 1 times his fish: the difference is 2 times his fish.
That difference is 12 fish.
2 times his fish = 12, so his fish = 6.
b2013-14.spot: 'Times as many' and 'more than' together? Compare the two amounts and take away what's the same.
b2013-14.oops: Dividing 12 by 3 = 4. The extra is 2 times the fish, not 3.

b2013-15.ask: A map shows how many cubes are in each tower. What do you see from the front?
steps: From the front, in each column you only see the TALLEST tower. Shorter ones hide behind it.
Column 1: 4, 3, 2, 1. Tallest 4.
Column 2: 2, 3, 1, 2. Tallest 3. Column 3: 3, 1, 3, 1. Tallest 3.
Column 4: 2, 2, 1, 2. Tallest 2. Heights 4, 3, 3, 2.
b2013-15.check: Picture E shows heights 4, 3, 3, 2 from left to right. ✓
b2013-15.spot: Views of buildings? In each line of sight, only the tallest one counts.
b2013-15.oops: Reading the front row only, instead of the tallest in each column.

b2013-16.ask: Five candidates, all with different votes, 36 in total. The winner got 12 and the last got 4. How many did second place get?
steps: Take away the winner and last place: 36 − 12 − 4 = 20 votes for the other three.
Those three numbers must all be different, bigger than 4 and smaller than 12.
Smallest possible for 4th and 3rd places: 5 and 6. Then 2nd gets 20 − 11 = 9.
Or 4th 5 and 3rd 7: 2nd gets 8. Anything else doesn't fit. So 2nd place got 8 or 9.
b2013-16.spot: Different numbers adding to a total? Squeeze the smaller ones as small as possible and see what's left.
b2013-16.oops: Finding one answer and stopping. Check if another works too.

b2013-17.ask: A small cube is cut out of every corner of a big wooden cube. How many faces does the new shape have?
steps: The big cube starts with 6 faces. Cutting corners doesn't remove any of them; they just get notches.
Each corner cut opens up 3 new little faces inside the notch.
A cube has 8 corners: 8 × 3 = 24 new faces.
b2013-17.check: Look at the picture: one cut corner shows 3 new small faces. ✓
b2013-17.spot: Cutting shapes? Count what's new at one spot, then multiply by how many spots.
b2013-17.oops: Thinking the old faces disappear. They're still there, just with bites taken out.

b2013-18.ask: How many pairs of two-digit numbers have a difference of exactly 50?
steps: The smaller number + 50 = the bigger number, and both must be two-digit (10 to 99).
Smallest small number: 10, paired with 60.
Biggest small number: 49, paired with 99. (50 would need 100, too big.)
From 10 to 49 there are 40 numbers, so 40 pairs.
b2013-18.spot: Counting pairs? Find the first and the last, then count everything in between.
b2013-18.oops: Counting 49 − 10 = 39 and forgetting to include both ends.

b2013-19.ask: 6 goals in the first half, guests leading. Then the home team scored 3 and won. How many goals did the home team score in total?
steps: First half: 6 goals, guests ahead. Possible scores (home : guests): 0 : 6, 1 : 5, 2 : 4.
Add 3 goals for the home team: 3 : 6, 4 : 5, 5 : 4.
Only 5 : 4 is a home win.
So the home team scored 2 + 3 = 5.
b2013-19.check: Half-time 2 : 4, guests lead. ✓ Final 5 : 4, home wins. ✓
b2013-19.spot: Only a few possibilities? List them all and check each against the clues.
b2013-19.oops: Forgetting the guests had to be ahead at half-time.

b2013-20.ask: In a 4 × 4 board, neighbouring numbers differ by 1. The top-left is 3 and a 9 is somewhere. How many different numbers are in the table?
steps: Moving one square changes the number by exactly 1.
To reach 9 from 3, you need 6 steps. The farthest square from the top-left corner is the bottom-right corner, exactly 6 steps away.
So 9 must be in the bottom-right, and every step along the way goes up by 1.
The numbers that appear are 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9: that's 7 different numbers.
b2013-20.check: Fill in: each square = 3 + (steps from the corner). Neighbours differ by 1 and the corner is 9. ✓
b2013-20.spot: Step-by-step changes on a grid? Count how many steps apart two squares are.
b2013-20.oops: Counting 9 − 3 = 6 and forgetting to count both 3 and 9.

b2013-21.ask: Aron, Bern and Carl always lie. Each has a red or green stone. Use their (false) sentences to find which statement is true.
steps: Aron's sentence is a lie, so Aron's colour is DIFFERENT from Bern's.
Bern's sentence is a lie, so Bern's colour is different from Carl's.
So Aron and Carl have the same colour, and Bern has the other colour. That means exactly two stones match.
Carl's lie: it's NOT true that exactly two are red. If Aron and Carl were red, that would make it true. So Aron and Carl are green, Bern is red.
b2013-21.check: Aron green, Bern red, Carl green. Every sentence is false. ✓
b2013-21.spot: Everyone lies? Turn each sentence around to get a true fact.

b2013-22.ask: 66 cats, 21 knocked out. Of the rest, 27 have stripes and 32 have one black ear. Cats with both go to the final. What's the fewest finalists?
steps: Cats left: 66 − 21 = 45.
If no cat had both, we'd need 27 + 32 = 59 cats. But there are only 45.
So some cats must be counted in both groups: 59 − 45 = 14 at least.
Those cats have stripes AND a black ear: at least 14 finalists.
b2013-22.check: 14 with both, 13 stripes only, 18 ear only: 14 + 13 + 18 = 45. ✓
b2013-22.spot: Two groups that don't fit side by side? The overlap is how much they spill over.
b2013-22.oops: Using all 66 cats instead of the 45 left.

b2013-23.ask: Four buttons: sad, happy, sad, happy. Pressing one flips it AND its neighbours. Fewest presses to make all happy?
steps: Try 1 press: none works. Try 2 presses: none works either.
Try 3 presses: press buttons 2, 3 and 4.
Press 2 (flips 1, 2, 3): happy, sad, happy, happy.
Press 3 (flips 2, 3, 4): happy, happy, sad, sad. Press 4 (flips 3, 4): happy, happy, happy, happy!
b2013-23.check: Follow the faces step by step and you end with all happy. ✓
b2013-23.spot: Stuck on a switches puzzle? Try it! One press, then two, then three, writing down the faces each time.
b2013-23.oops: Pressing the sad buttons directly. That also flips their happy neighbours.

b2013-24.ask: 40 boys and 28 girls stand in a circle holding hands. 18 boys give their right hand to a girl. How many boys give their left hand to a girl?
steps: Walk around the circle. Kids stand in groups: some boys together, then some girls together, then boys again, and so on.
Every group of girls has a boy on its left end and a boy on its right end.
At one end a boy gives his right hand to a girl; at the other end a boy gives his left hand.
So the counts are always equal: 18 and 18.
b2013-24.check: Try a small circle: B B G B G. Count right-hand-to-girl and left-hand-to-girl: they're equal. ✓
b2013-24.spot: Things in a circle? Look at where one group stops and another starts.
b2013-24.oops: Using the numbers 40 and 28. They don't matter here.

b2013-25.ask: Build a 2 × 2 × 2 cube from 4 white and 4 black small cubes. How many really different cubes can you make? (Turning doesn't count as different.)
steps: Turn the cube so the bottom layer has as many white cubes as possible, then sort.
4 white on the bottom: the top is all black. 1 way.
3 white on the bottom (best you can do): the one top white can sit in different spots relative to the bottom black cube. Careful listing gives 4 different cubes.
At most 2 white on every face (like a checkerboard pattern): 2 more different cubes.
b2013-25.check: Build them with real blocks or sugar cubes and try turning each to match another. You'll find 7 that never match. ✓
b2013-25.spot: Counting things that can turn? Pick a rule (like 'most white on the bottom') so you don't count the same cube twice.
b2013-25.oops: Counting two cubes as different when one is just the other turned around.

b2013-26.ask: A 3-digit number minus 297 gives the same digits reversed. How many such numbers are there?
steps: Write the number as abc. Its reverse is cba.
abc − cba always equals 99 × (a − c). Try it: 512 − 215 = 297 = 99 × 3.
cba must be a 3-digit number, so c can't be 0. Pairs: (4,1), (5,2), (6,3), (7,4), (8,5), (9,6): 6 pairs.
The middle digit b can be anything from 0 to 9: 10 choices. 6 × 10 = 60.
b2013-26.spot: Reversed digits? Write the number by place value: hundreds, tens, ones.
b2013-26.oops: Forgetting the middle digit can be anything.

b2013-27.ask: 8 curved pieces make a circle. Marten starts with two pieces bending opposite ways. Fewest pieces for a closed track?
steps: 8 pieces make a full circle, so 4 pieces make a half circle.
Cut Matthew's circle into its two half circles and pull them apart.
Marten's two starting pieces (one bending each way) make a wiggle that shifts the track sideways. Put one wiggle on each side between the half circles: 2 + 2 = 4 pieces.
8 + 4 = 12 pieces make a closed track.
b2013-27.check: Sketch it: half circle, wiggle, half circle, wiggle, back to the start. 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 12. ✓
b2013-27.spot: Track and path puzzles? Break the shape into parts you know, like half circles.
b2013-27.oops: Answering 8. The opposite bend at the start forces extra pieces.

b2013-28.ask: 2013 islanders, knights (truthful) and liars. Each day one says 'After I leave, knights will equal liars', then leaves. After 2013 days no one is left. How many liars at the start?
steps: Rewind! Start with the very last person. After they leave there are 0 knights and 0 liars: equal. So their sentence is TRUE: a knight.
Second-last person: after leaving, 1 knight and 0 liars remain. Not equal: FALSE. A liar.
Third-last: after leaving, 1 knight and 1 liar. Equal: TRUE. A knight.
The pattern goes knight, liar, knight, liar... from the end. 2013 people: 1007 knights and 1006 liars.
b2013-28.spot: Events that happen one by one until the end? Rewind and start from the last one.
b2013-28.oops: Starting from the first person, where you don't know anything yet.

b2013-29.ask: 'Change-sum' replaces each number with the sum of the other two. Starting from 20, 1, 3 and doing it 2013 times, what's the biggest difference between two numbers?
steps: Try it once: 20, 1, 3 becomes 4, 23, 21.
The differences stay the same each time! (Each number swaps places with the others' sum, so gaps just flip.)
The biggest difference is always 19.
b2013-29.check: Do it once more: 4, 23, 21 → 44, 25, 27. Biggest difference 44 − 25 = 19. ✓
b2013-29.spot: A step repeated many times? Do it a few times and look for what never changes.

b2013-30.ask: Four dice-like cubes (made from the net shown) are glued into a 2 × 2 × 1 block, matching numbers glued together. What's the biggest total on the outside?
steps: From the net, opposite faces are 3 and 5, 6 and 4, 1 and 2. Each cube adds to 21.
In the block, each cube hides 2 faces that are next to each other (not opposite).
To keep the outside big, hide the smallest numbers. 1 and 3 are next to each other: hide those.
Glue the cubes so every joint is 1-to-1 or 3-to-3. Each cube then shows 21 − 4 = 17.
b2013-30.check: Hiding 1 and 2 would be smaller, but they're opposite faces and can't both touch neighbours. So 1 + 3 is the best. ✓
b2013-30.spot: Biggest outside total? Squeeze the hidden numbers as small as possible, and check it's allowed.
b2013-30.oops: Hiding 1 and 2. They're on opposite sides of the cube.
